_note: Minting: refined metal alloyed to the coin's fineness, cast into flans and struck or cast in moulds. A recipe with actor "mint" is run by the mint, not by firms: the coin standard names it (mint_recipe) and the mint (sim/economy/mint.py, mint_labour.py) hires its labour hours per kilogram of coin; the fine metal comes from the standard's fineness, and the metal inputs here are the reference alloy the price solver prices. The mint's charge (seigniorage) is not a cost of this process; it is the coin standard's mint_charge_share. Complaints/374.

struck_silver_coin_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of struck silver coin of eight parts silver to two of copper by mass
struck_silver_coin_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D) for the labour and fuel; the process is attested. The silver and copper are the coin's fineness (the post-reform denarius is put near 80 percent silver by Butcher and Ponting, the figure in rome_100ad's coin_standard); metal lost in melting is not charged. Striking: a hammer-struck flan takes a striker and a holder, taken at five coins a minute for the pair, so 150 coins per labourer-hour; at the coin's gross mass (the fine silver in the standard over the fineness) that is about 0.5 kg of coin per labourer-hour, 2100 hours per tonne with trimming and sorting. Melting, alloying and casting flans: furnaceman hours per tonne are about 0.8 per kg (a crucible charge of a few kilograms per hour). Charcoal: heat to melt silver and copper is a fraction of a megajoule per kg, a small crucible furnace delivers a few percent of the fuel's heat, so about 0.2 kg of charcoal per kg of coin. Dies: an engraver cuts a die pair in about a day and a die pair strikes some tens of thousands of coins; 320 hours per tonne is that ratio rounded. Pass 11 source for the striking rate: Lawrence University (Buerger), 'Striking the coins', http://www2.lawrence.edu/dept/art/BUERGER/ESSAYS/PRODUCTION7.HTML, opened: a modern experimenter could 'strike 100 coins an hour, including casting the blanks', alone, and Roman misstrikes suggest 'as much as one coin every three seconds' (1200 an hour) with a crew of three or four; the 150 coins per labourer-hour here sits between. Pass 12 DIES: Lawrence University (Buerger), 'Making the dies' (https://www2.lawrence.edu/dept/art/BUERGER/ESSAYS/PRODUCTION6.HTML, opened): 'an obverse die could strike about 15,000 acceptable coins, a reverse die only about half as many' (modern experiments), and one nineteenth-century counterfeiter took 18 hours to copy a complex die; The E-Sylum (https://coinbooks.org/esylum_v17n20a12.html, opened) implies two dies a day for an engraver. Arithmetic: a tonne at 3.3 g a coin (the 0.5 kg per labourer-hour above over 150 coins an hour) is 300,000 coins, so 300,000 / 15,000 = 20 obverse dies and 300,000 / 7,500 = 40 reverse dies, 60 dies; at half a day (4 hours of an 8-hour day) each that is 240 engraver hours, at 18 hours each 1,080; the 320 here sits inside that range, kept. CHARCOAL, derived: heat to take a kilogram of the 80/20 alloy from 20 C to melting is 7.42 mol of silver at (25.35 J/mol/K * 942 K + 11.28 kJ/mol) plus 3.15 mol of copper at (24.44 * 1065 + 13.26 kJ/mol), about 261 + 124 = 385 kJ (Wikipedia, Silver and Copper, opened: melting points 1234.93 K and 1357.77 K, heats of fusion 11.28 and 13.26 kJ/mol, molar heat capacities 25.350 and 24.440 J/mol/K; superheat and alloy melting-point depression ignored); carbon gives at most 32.8 MJ/kg (Wikipedia, Heat of combustion, opened, graphite; charcoal's own value was not found); Idris and others, UNIOSUN Journal of Engineering and Environmental Sciences 7(1), 2025 (https://journals.uniosun.edu.ng/ujees/article/download/417/378/746, opened as text) measured 'a thermal efficiency of 14%' for a small crucible furnace (a modern analogue, coal-fired, aluminium). At 14 percent the fuel is 0.385 / (0.14 * 32.8) = 0.084 kg of charcoal per kg of coin, at an ASSUMED 5 percent for an open ancient furnace 0.24; the 0.2 here lies in that range. Still unsourced: furnaceman hours and the 8 to 2 silver to copper split beyond the cited fineness; so conf stays D.

cast_bronze_cash_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of cast bronze cash
cast_bronze_cash_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (conf D) for the labour and fuel; the process is attested (cash cast in clay or bronze moulds, many to a tree, broken off, filed and strung). Melting and pouring: furnaceman hours per tonne are about half a furnaceman-hour per kg at a few kilograms a crucible charge. Breaking off, filing the rim and stringing, at a few hundred coins an hour for a worker, about 3 g a coin: nearly a kilogram an hour, 900 hours per tonne with mould making. Charcoal: heat to melt bronze is a fraction of a megajoule per kg and a small furnace delivers a few percent of the fuel's heat, so about 0.3 kg of charcoal per kg of cash. Pass 11: the Lawrence University essay (http://www2.lawrence.edu/dept/art/BUERGER/ESSAYS/PRODUCTION7.HTML, opened) gives 100 struck coins an hour including casting the blanks, for hammered coin, not cast cash; no source found for cash filing and stringing rates or furnaceman hours, so conf stays D. Pass 12 CHARCOAL, derived as for the silver coin: copper at 24.44 J/mol/K * 1065 K + 13.26 kJ/mol is 39.3 kJ/mol over 63.546 g/mol, 0.62 MJ per kg of metal (bronze taken as copper; Wikipedia, Copper, opened); at 32.8 MJ/kg of charcoal at most and a furnace efficiency of 14 percent (Idris and others 2025, UNIOSUN, opened, a modern analogue) that is 0.13 kg per kg, at an ASSUMED 5 percent 0.38; the 0.3 here lies in that range.
